cards.front: {{c1::Ecological succession}} is the change, over years to centuries, in which species live in an area.
cards.quote: Ecological succession is the change, over years to centuries, in which species live there.

cards.front: In ecology, what is a community?
cards.back: All the populations of different species living in one area.
cards.quote: A community is all the populations of different species living in one area.

cards.front: Besides changed conditions, what else shapes the path of succession in a recovering plant community?
cards.back: Which seeds arrive, and plants that hold newcomers back. So succession is a tendency, not one fixed species list, timetable or endpoint for every place.
cards.quote: Changed conditions are not the only driver: which seeds arrive, and plants that hold newcomers back, also shape the path.

cards.front: In a succession simulation, an abandoned field has grown into forest, and then half the plot is burned. What grows first on the burned half, and is it primary or secondary succession?
cards.back: Weeds, grasses and seeds already in the soil come first. A fire leaves the soil in place, so this is secondary succession, not a restart from bare rock.
cards.why: Soil still holds nutrients, seeds and roots after a disturbance like fire.
cards.quote: Predict 1. Let the field reach forest, then burn or clear only half.
cards.section: Explore: run a field through the decades

cards.front: A {{c1::disturbance}} is an event such as fire, flood, storm or plowing that removes much of a community.
cards.quote: Succession often starts after a disturbance, an event such as fire, flood, storm or plowing that removes much of a community.
cards.section: What the starting surface changes

cards.front: {{c1::Primary succession}} is succession on bare rock or new land where there is no soil.
cards.quote: Primary succession is succession on bare rock or new land where there is no soil.
cards.section: What the starting surface changes

cards.front: On bare rock, which organisms are usually the pioneer species?
cards.back: Lichens and mosses.
cards.quote: On bare rock they are usually lichens and mosses.
cards.section: What the starting surface changes

cards.front: How do lichens and mosses prepare bare rock for later plants?
cards.back: They help break down the rock, and when they die they add the first thin layer of soil.
cards.quote: They help break down the rock, and when they die they add the first thin layer of soil.
cards.section: What the starting surface changes

cards.front: {{c1::Secondary succession}} is succession after a disturbance that leaves the soil in place.
cards.quote: Secondary succession is succession after a disturbance that leaves the soil in place.
cards.section: What the starting surface changes

cards.front: A volcano builds new land from fresh lava, and a flood drowns a meadow but leaves its soil. Which event starts primary succession and which starts secondary succession?
cards.back: The fresh lava starts primary succession because there is no soil. The flooded meadow starts secondary succession because its soil remains.
cards.quote: Bare rock, sand and silt left by a melting glacier and fresh lava are examples.
cards.section: What the starting surface changes

cards.front: A fire burns a Virginia forest, and a glacier melts back from bare rock. Which area should recover its plant cover sooner, and why?
cards.back: The burned forest usually recovers sooner, because secondary succession starts with soil that still holds nutrients, seeds and roots. Primary succession must first build soil.
cards.quote: Examples are an abandoned farm field, a burned forest and a flooded meadow, where the soil still holds nutrients, seeds and roots.
cards.section: What the starting surface changes

cards.front: On the poor new soil left by a retreating glacier, how does alder help later plants?
cards.back: Alder adds nitrogen to the poor new soil.
cards.quote: On the gravel and silt a glacier leaves, hardy plants such as Dryas also come early, and plants such as alder add nitrogen to the poor new soil.
cards.section: What the starting surface changes

cards.front: {{c1::Abiotic factors}} are nonliving parts of an ecosystem, such as light, water, temperature and soil.
cards.quote: Abiotic factors are nonliving parts of an ecosystem, such as light, water, temperature and soil.
cards.section: How a Virginia field can become a forest

cards.front: How can plants in a community both help and hold back other plants as succession proceeds?
cards.back: Plants change abiotic factors by growing and dying. Those changes can help later plants, but plants already present can also hold newcomers back.
cards.quote: Plants change abiotic factors by growing and dying. Those changes can help later plants, while plants already present can also hold newcomers back.
cards.section: How a Virginia field can become a forest

cards.front: In a Piedmont old field, what plants dominate during the first three years after farming stops, and in what order?
cards.back: Fast-growing weeds such as horseweed and asters come first in full sun. By about the third year, broomsedge, a tall grass, often covers the field.
cards.quote: By about the third year, broomsedge, a tall grass, often covers the field.
cards.section: How a Virginia field can become a forest

cards.front: In a published summary of Piedmont old fields, pines arrive during years 3 to 18, but a young pine forest dominates during years 19 to 30. Why are those two not the same event?
cards.back: Pines appear first and then need years to grow tall enough to dominate. Arriving and dominating are different stages.
cards.quote: Pines appear first and take years to grow tall enough to dominate.
cards.section: How a Virginia field can become a forest

cards.front: Why do shade-tolerant trees such as red maple, not young pines, do best under a closed pine canopy?
cards.back: Pines grow fast in full sun, but the canopy shades the ground. Shade-tolerant trees such as red maple do best there, and oaks and hickories survive some shade and grow best in gaps with more light.
cards.quote: Oaks and hickories can survive some shade, but they grow best where a gap lets in light.
cards.section: How a Virginia field can become a forest

cards.front: In old-field succession, how do hardwoods take over from pines?
cards.back: As the old pines die over several decades, the hardwoods growing below fill the gaps.
cards.quote: As the old pines die over the next several decades, the hardwoods below fill the gaps.
cards.section: How a Virginia field can become a forest

cards.front: The {{c1::climax community}} is the late stage that the model predicts will stay fairly stable without a major disturbance. For most of Virginia the model names oak-hickory forest.
cards.quote: The climax community is the late stage that the model predicts will stay fairly stable without a major disturbance.
cards.section: How a Virginia field can become a forest

cards.front: A Piedmont field is abandoned and nothing disturbs it. About how long before hardwoods dominate, and what forest does the model predict at the end?
cards.back: After a century or more, hardwoods dominate. The model's late stage for most of Virginia is oak-hickory forest.
cards.quote: After a century or more, hardwoods dominate, and one Virginia source puts a mostly hardwood forest at about 200 years.
cards.section: How a Virginia field can become a forest

cards.front: An eastern forest has gone without fire for decades, and red maple seedlings are common under the oaks. Predict what may happen to the canopy, and what would open the canopy for young oaks.
cards.back: Red maple and other shade-tolerant trees may replace the oaks, as in many eastern forests left without fire, because young oaks need more light than a closed canopy provides. A disturbance that opens gaps in the canopy would let in light for oaks.
cards.why: Rests on: oak seedlings need gaps, and shade-tolerant trees do not.
cards.quote: In many eastern forests left without fire, red maple and other shade-tolerant trees are replacing oaks because young oaks need more light than a closed canopy provides.
cards.section: How a Virginia field can become a forest

cards.front: A North Carolina experiment gave forest plots no change, cutting, fire alone, or cutting plus fire. If fire alone helped young oaks, what should the fire-alone plots show compared with the untreated plots?
cards.back: More young oak saplings than the untreated plots. In the experiment, fire alone did not show this.
cards.quote: A North Carolina experiment gave forest plots no change, cutting, fire alone, or cutting plus fire.
cards.section: Disturbance keeps the story open

cards.front: In the North Carolina forest experiment, which treatment reduced the big trees, and what happened to young oak saplings?
cards.back: Only cutting plus fire reduced the total trunk area of the big trees, and young oak saplings were more common where the most was lost. The smallest oak seedlings showed no clear difference, so the effect depended on treatment and plant size.
cards.quote: Only cutting plus fire reduced the total trunk area of the big trees, and young oak saplings were more common where the most was lost.
cards.section: Disturbance keeps the story open

cards.front: Why can one landscape hold a patchwork of succession stages?
cards.back: Disturbances reset parts of a landscape, so succession can start over in patches. Fire can sometimes favor certain species.
cards.quote: Disturbances reset parts of a landscape, so succession can start over in patches, and fire can sometimes favor certain species.
cards.section: Disturbance keeps the story open

cards.front: {{c1::Biodiversity}} is the variety of living things in an area, and succession changes it.
cards.quote: Succession also changes biodiversity, the variety of living things in an area.
cards.section: Disturbance keeps the story open

cards.front: At Glacier Bay plot Q2 in Alaska, ice left bare ground in 1879, and the oldest spruce found there began growing in 1960. How many years elapsed before that spruce began growing?
cards.quote: At plot Q2, calculate the elapsed time before the oldest spruce found there began growing.
cards.section: Two timelines, two kinds of evidence

cards.front: Glacier Bay plot Q2 was the only one of eight plots to become spruce-dominated without ever having alder. What claim about all of Glacier Bay can Q2 not support?
cards.back: That Glacier Bay plots usually get spruce at about 81 years, or that spruce follows alder there. Q2 supports only a narrow claim about one dated place.
cards.why: Rests on: one plot is one history, and it was the exception among eight plots.
cards.quote: Q2 cannot show that Glacier Bay plots usually get spruce at about 81 years, or that spruce follows alder there.
cards.section: Two timelines, two kinds of evidence

cards.front: A table lists Piedmont old-field stages, Glacier Bay plot Q2 dates, and a park's about-80 and about-200 year story. Which rows are measured at one dated place, and how should that change your trust in each kind?
cards.back: Plot Q2's rows come from one dated plot, so they are specific but apply to that place. The Piedmont rows are a regional summary with no observation dates, and the park rows are estimates, not measured. Trust summaries and estimates less for exact timing.
cards.quote: Which rows come from one dated place, and which are a summary or an illustration?
cards.section: Two timelines, two kinds of evidence

cards.front: Design a fair test of whether shade slows the growth of pine seedlings more than oak seedlings, using potted seedlings, shade cloth and a ruler. Name the variables, the control and the sample size.
cards.back: Independent variables: light (full sun or shade cloth) and kind of seedling (pine or oak). Dependent variable: height gain in cm after 8 weeks. Constants: pot size, soil, water, starting height, place. Control: full sun for each kind. At least 10 seedlings per group.
cards.quote: Plan a fair test of whether shade slows the growth of pine seedlings more than oak seedlings, using seedlings in pots, shade cloth and a ruler.
cards.section: Design problem
